# Assumptions of linear regression {#sec-linear-regression-assumptions}

















We ended the last chapter admitting something uncomfortable out loud: the line in @fig-what_intercept_slope, drawn straight across every DPI from 0 to 30, is almost certainly the wrong model for how tissue area actually behaves after ischemia. We said we'd come back to that. This is us coming back to it.

Here's the part nobody's computer will ever tell them: `lm()` and `brm()` don't check whether a straight line makes sense for your data before fitting one; they just fit it, coefficients and all, whether or not the result means anything. Five assumptions decide whether those coefficients are worth trusting: linearity, independence, homoscedasticity, normality of the residuals, and no multicollinearity. None of them get checked automatically. That job is yours, and it's the whole subject of this chapter.

::: callout-warning
Neither R, `brms`, SPSS, nor STATA will pop up a warning window telling you your assumptions are violated. Verifying them is a modeling step, not an afterthought, as much a part of "fitting a model" as writing the formula.
:::

::: callout-tip
## The five assumptions we'll check

- Linearity
- Independence
- Homoscedasticity
- Normality of residuals
- No multicollinearity
:::

## Linearity

Think about your own weight over your lifetime. From birth through childhood, it climbs at a fairly steady clip: roughly one straight line, age in, weight out. Push that same line into adolescence, adulthood, and beyond, though, and it falls apart: diet, activity, metabolism, and a dozen other things start pulling weight around in ways age alone can't predict, and the trajectory plateaus, wobbles, sometimes reverses. The relationship didn't stop being real. It stopped being a *straight* one. That's linearity as an assumption, not as a definition: a linear regression doesn't ask "is $x$ related to $y$?" It assumes the specific shape of that relationship is a straight line, given by @eq-linear-regression-simple, and everything downstream (the coefficients, their uncertainty, any prediction you make from them) inherits that assumption whether it's true or not.

You've already watched this assumption fail, on real data, in the last chapter. @fig-what_intercept_slope fit one straight line across the full 0–30 DPI range of `cell_data`, and we flagged (without proving it yet) that this was probably the wrong call. Let's prove it. Here's that exact model:








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linearity_model <- lm(Tisue_Area ~ DPI, data = cell_data)
```
:::








If the straight-line assumption held, the residuals (what's left over after the line's prediction is subtracted from the real value) should scatter randomly around zero with no discernible shape. If they trace a curve instead, that curve is the line telling you exactly how it's wrong.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data.frame(fitted = fitted(linearity_model), residuals = residuals(linearity_model)),
       aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.6, size = 2) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, color = "#D55E00") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Fitted tissue area", y = "Residual (observed − fitted)") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Residuals from the full-range DPI model, against fitted values](linear-regression-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-assumptions_linearity_residuals-1.png){#fig-assumptions_linearity_residuals width=672}
:::
:::








That's not random scatter; it's a bow. And once you know the biology, the bow makes complete sense: ischemic tissue doesn't just shrink monotonically from day 0 onward. The group means tell the real story: tissue area actually rises slightly by DPI 3 (acute edema, swelling from the injury itself) before falling through DPI 7, 14, and 30 as neurodegeneration takes over. A single straight line, forced to summarize a rise-then-fall with one slope, splits the difference badly at both ends, which is exactly the curved residual pattern in @fig-assumptions_linearity_residuals. Recognizing that shape as "acute edema, then atrophy" rather than just "bad fit" is the part no software does for you: it takes knowing what ischemic tissue actually does over three decades of days, which is your job, not `lm()`'s.

::: callout-tip
Real biological relationships are under no obligation to be straight lines, and forcing one onto a curve doesn't just fit slightly worse; it can point the slope itself in a misleading direction. Knowing your system's biology well enough to *expect* a shape like this before you even plot it is what separates a diagnostic check from a guessing game.
:::

A tempting fix here (and one plenty of tutorials reach for immediately) is a log or square-root transform to force curvature into a straight line. I'd rather not reach for that by default. Pablo Inchausti calls these "esoteric transformations" [@inchausti2023], and I agree with his objection: they often buy linearity at the cost of interpretability, leaving you with coefficients for "log tissue area" that no longer mean anything to a biologist. Now that you have tools built for exactly this (nonlinear and multilevel models, covered properly in @sec-longitudinal-timeseries), reaching for a distorting transformation is rarely the best option available to you anymore.

## Independence

Independence asks something different: not whether the *shape* of the relationship is right, but whether each observation is actually giving you new information, or just echoing a neighbor. Formally, it requires the error terms $\epsilon$ to be uncorrelated across observations. Picture a mouse run three times on a rotarod, with the time-to-fall recorded each time. Those three numbers aren't three independent draws; they're one mouse's motor learning curve sampled three times, and treating them as independent observations quietly triples your apparent sample size without earning it.

This should sound familiar, because `cell_data` has exactly this structure baked in: cells nested in tissue sections nested in animals. A model that treats every cell as an independent observation is making the same mistake as the rotarod example, just one level removed from where it's easy to see, which is precisely the problem @sec-multilevel-varying-intercepts exists to fix properly, once you have the machinery (varying intercepts) that fixing it actually requires. For now, a small simulation makes the failure mode visible without needing that machinery yet.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(8807)
time_steps <- seq(1, 100, by = 1)

response_independent <- 5 + 0.3 * time_steps + rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 5)

response_dependent <- numeric(100)
response_dependent[1] <- 5 + rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = 5)
for (i in 2:100) {
  response_dependent[i] <- 5 + 0.3 * time_steps[i] +
    0.8 * response_dependent[i - 1] + rnorm(1, mean = 0, sd = 5)
}

data_independence <- rbind(
  data.frame(time = time_steps, response = response_independent, type = "Independent"),
  data.frame(time = time_steps, response = response_dependent, type = "Dependent (autocorrelated)")
)

ggplot(data_independence, aes(x = time, y = response)) +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2") +
  facet_wrap(~type) +
  labs(x = "Time", y = "Response") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Independent vs. autocorrelated observations over time](linear-regression-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-assumptions_independence-1.png){#fig-assumptions_independence width=672}
:::
:::








Both panels were generated with the same underlying trend and the same noise level. The independent panel looks like what it is: noisy, but going nowhere it shouldn't. The dependent panel, where each point is partly just 80% of the last one plus a little more trend, looks like a rising stock instead: a trajectory, not scatter. Fit a naive linear model to that second panel treating every point as independent, and you'll get a tight, confident-looking effect of time that is substantially overstating how much evidence you actually have. This is not a rare mistake: repeated measures from the same animal, subject, or preparation get treated as independent observations often enough that it's worth naming as its own failure mode, separate from "wrong shape" or "wrong variance."

## Homoscedasticity

Homoscedasticity asks whether the residuals' *spread* stays constant across the predictor's range: whether the model is equally uncertain everywhere, or confidently right in some regions and badly wrong in others. It matters because every credible interval and standard error your model reports is computed assuming that spread is constant; when it isn't, those intervals are too narrow in the high-variance regions and too wide in the low-variance ones, and you have no way of knowing which is which without checking.

We don't need a synthetic example for this one: `linearity_model`'s own residuals already show it, just sliced a different way than before: by DPI group instead of by fitted value.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data.frame(DPI = factor(cell_data$DPI), residuals = residuals(linearity_model)),
       aes(x = DPI, y = residuals)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.6, color = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  labs(x = "Days post-injury (DPI)", y = "Residual (observed − fitted)") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Residual spread by DPI group](linear-regression-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-assumptions_homoscedasticity-1.png){#fig-assumptions_homoscedasticity width=672}
:::
:::








This won't look like the textbook funnel you'll see in most references: DPI only takes five discrete values here, not a continuous sweep. But the diagnostic question is identical: is the spread the same at every value of the predictor? It isn't. Day 3 shows visibly wider scatter than day 0, 7, 14, or 30, which tracks with what @sec-eda-ggplot already showed you about this dataset, and with the biology: the acute post-ischemic window is when individual animals diverge most from each other, before the injury's trajectory settles into something more predictable. A model that reports one uncertainty number for the whole 0–30 day range is quietly averaging over that: too confident about day 3, probably too cautious about day 30.

Rather than reach for a log transform here either, the more direct fix is to let the model's variance itself depend on the predictor: a distributional model, which we'll build properly in @sec-multivariate-distributional-regression once you've seen the rest of the multilevel toolkit. The short version worth holding onto for now: heteroscedasticity isn't a defect to transform away, it's information about where your data is more and less trustworthy, and a model that can say so explicitly is strictly more honest than one that can't.

## Normality of residuals

The normality assumption is narrower than it sounds, and it's worth being precise about what it does and doesn't cover: it's a statement about the *residuals* (the leftover error), not about the predictors, and not about the raw response variable itself.

::: callout-warning
Normality applies to the model's residuals, not to the predictors or the response. A skewed response can still produce nicely normal residuals once the model accounts for what's driving that skew, and, as you're about to see, residuals can look normal even when something else about the model is badly wrong.
:::

Here's a genuinely useful, slightly humbling thing to notice: the same `linearity_model` we just used to demonstrate two separate problems (a curved relationship it can't capture, and variance that isn't constant) still produces residuals that look, well, fine.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data.frame(residuals = residuals(linearity_model)), aes(x = residuals)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.8, color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Residual", y = "Count") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Histogram of residuals from the full-range DPI model](linear-regression-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-assumptions_normality_hist-1.png){#fig-assumptions_normality_hist width=672}
:::
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(data.frame(residuals = residuals(linearity_model)), aes(sample = residuals)) +
  stat_qq(color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "#D55E00") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Q-Q plot of residuals from the full-range DPI model](linear-regression-assumptions_files/figure-html/fig-assumptions_normality_qq-1.png){#fig-assumptions_normality_qq width=672}
:::
:::








Both figures look close to what a well-behaved normal residual should look like (a roughly bell-shaped histogram, points hugging the diagonal in the Q-Q plot) and a Shapiro-Wilk test agrees ($W = 0.97$, $p = 0.36$, no evidence against normality). And yet we know for a fact this model is misspecified: we just spent two sections proving its linearity and homoscedasticity assumptions both fail. That's the point worth sitting with. Normality is checking one specific thing, and it has nothing useful to say about whether the *shape* of your model is right. A residual histogram that looks like a perfect bell curve is not a clean bill of health; it's one assumption cleared out of five, no more and no less.

So why doesn't this book spend more time on residual normality? Because $\hat{\beta}_0$ and $\hat{\beta}_1$ are themselves weighted averages of the data, and a weighted average of enough observations tends toward a normal sampling distribution by the central limit theorem, regardless of how the individual residuals are shaped: skewed, bimodal, whatever. That's why Gelman, Hill, and Vehtari are comfortable saying, bluntly, that "for the purpose of estimating the regression line (as compared to predicting individual data points), the assumption of normality is typically barely important at all" [@gelman2020], and it's the same reason Inchausti treats minor departures from normality as tolerable once your sample size is reasonable [@inchausti2023]. The one place this protection genuinely runs out is when your goal shifts from estimating the line itself to predicting where one *new*, individual animal will land: an individual prediction interval depends on the actual shape of the residual tail, not just the mean, and no amount of sample size fixes that if the tail is badly behaved.

::: {#fig-fitmodels layout-ncol="1"}
![](images/model_fit.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"}

There are, broadly, two ways to respond to a model that doesn't quite fit. One is the ritualistic option: keep using the same linear regression regardless of what the data actually looks like, and stretch its robustness as far as it'll go. The other is to become the kind of modeling tailor who reaches for the tool built for the shape of the data in front of them: nonlinear terms, varying variance, whatever the biology actually calls for. Over the next few chapters, you'll have an entire wardrobe to choose from. There's rarely a good reason to keep reaching for the one ill-fitting suit.
:::

For outcomes where normal residuals genuinely aren't realistic to expect (reaction times with a long right tail, for instance), @sec-beta-robust-regression covers robust alternatives like Student-t regression directly, rather than asking you to force normality onto data that was never going to give it to you.

## No multicollinearity

The last assumption only comes up once you have two or more predictors: multicollinearity, where predictors are correlated highly enough that they're carrying largely redundant information about the response. Knowing one predictor's value then tells you most of what you'd need to know about the other, which makes it hard for the model to credit either one individually: coefficients become unstable, and their standard errors inflate, even though the model's overall fit might look fine.

::: callout-note
### A naming note before we go further

This section uses `Tissue_Area`, not the `Tisue_Area` column the rest of this chapter has been using. They're not the same measurement expressed two ways by coincidence: a look at the raw CSV shows `Tisue_Area` is `Tissue_Area` scaled by exactly $10^6$, almost certainly a leftover unit-conversion duplicate in the data. We're using `Tissue_Area` here only because it's the column already alongside the PDGFR-β/GFAP predictors below; the scale doesn't change anything about how VIF is interpreted.
:::

You've already done the legwork for this one, back in @sec-eda-ggpairs: a pairwise correlation matrix on this dataset showed `Pdgfrb_Area`/`Pdgfrb_IntDen` and `Gfap_Area`/`Gfap_IntDen` each highly correlated (Pearson's $r$ of 0.94 and 0.98, respectively); each pair carries largely redundant information. That was a general finding, made before any model was on the table. With an actual regression model in front of us, the question sharpens from "are these correlated?" to "how much is that correlation distorting *this* model's coefficients?" That is what the variance inflation factor (VIF) answers directly.








::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cell_data_sub <- subset(cell_data, select = c(Tissue_Area, Pdgfrb_Area, Pdgfrb_IntDen, Gfap_Area, Gfap_IntDen))
```
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(car)

model <- lm(Tissue_Area ~ Pdgfrb_Area + Gfap_Area + Gfap_IntDen, data = cell_data_sub)

vif_values <- vif(model)
vif_values
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Pdgfrb_Area   Gfap_Area Gfap_IntDen 
    1.74181    47.37687    50.03761 
```


:::
:::








`Gfap_Area` and `Gfap_IntDen` both carry an extremely large VIF (around 50), against 1.7 for `Pdgfrb_Area` [@car]. Past the conventional threshold of 5, and well past 10, that's not a subtle warning; it's the two GFAP predictors actively fighting each other for credit over the same underlying signal.

The most direct fix is simply to drop one. Including both `Gfap_Area` and `Gfap_IntDen` adds no real information the model didn't already have from the other, while inflating standard errors and destabilizing both coefficients. Which one to drop is a judgment call, not a statistical one: weigh which is easier to measure reliably, which is more interpretable for your specific question, and which better matches the biological quantity you actually care about. (If you ever find yourself choosing between age and a genuine preference for pistachio gelato as competing predictors, go with age; it generalizes better across studies.) Feature engineering [@kuhn2021] (building a new composite variable from the correlated pair instead of just discarding one) is the other real option, and one we'll return to once multiple-predictor models are the norm rather than the exception.

::: callout-tip
When multicollinearity forces a choice, favor the predictor that's easier to measure reliably and more directly tied to the biological question, not just whichever has the smaller VIF.
:::

## Where this leaves us

Five assumptions, one running example: a single straight line across the full DPI range of `cell_data`, which we now know fails linearity, fails homoscedasticity, and, despite both of those failures, still passes a normality check clean enough to fool you if it were the only thing you looked at. That's the real lesson of this chapter, more than any one assumption on its own: these checks aren't independent boxes to tick, and passing one tells you nothing about the others.

None of this means the line from @fig-what_intercept_slope was a wasted exercise, and it doesn't mean linear regression is the wrong tool for this dataset. It means the *full* 0–30 DPI range was the wrong range to ask it to cover in one go. @sec-linear-regression-single-continuous picks this exact model back up, does the one thing this chapter's diagnostics recommend (restrict the range to where a straight line is actually a defensible description of the biology) and, unlike this chapter, takes it all the way through to a fitted, interpreted, `brms`-and-`parsnip` model with something to say about the effect of time on tissue area.
